exercises.title: Is a vector in the span?
exercises.description: Does $\vec w = (5,7)$ lie in $\operatorname{span}\{(1,1),(1,2)\}$? If so, give the linear combination.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\vec w$ lies in the span if there are scalars $a,b$ with $a(1,1) + b(1,2) = (5,7)$. This is a linear system.

Step 2: System of equations
$a + b = 5$ and $a + 2b = 7$.

Step 3: Solve
Subtracting: $b = 2$, then $a = 3$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
Since the two vectors are linearly independent ($\det\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} = 1 \neq 0$) they span all of $\mathbb{R}^2$: every vector lies in the span. The question becomes interesting for dependent vectors.

exercises.title: Subspace or not?
exercises.description: Decide which sets are subspaces: (a) $U = \{(x,y,z) \mid x = y\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$, (b) $V = \{(x,y) \mid xy = 0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We check the zero vector, closure under addition and under scalar multiplication; for non-subspaces a counterexample suffices.

Step 2: (a) Subspace
$(0,0,0) \in U$. If $(a,a,c)$ and $(b,b,d)$ are in $U$ then the sum $(a+b,\ a+b,\ c+d) \in U$ and $\lambda(a,a,c) = (\lambda a,\lambda a,\lambda c) \in U$. Basis: $(1,1,0)$, $(0,0,1)$; $\dim U = 2$ (a plane through the origin).

Step 3: (b) not a subspace
$(1,0) \in V$ and $(0,1) \in V$ (since $1\cdot0 = 0$) but the sum $(1,1)$ has $1\cdot1 = 1 \neq 0$, so $(1,1) \notin V$. Not closed under addition.

Step 4: Geometric interpretation
$V$ is the union of the two coordinate axes. The union of two subspaces is a subspace only if one lies in the other.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
(Homogeneous) linear equations define subspaces, nonlinear conditions like $xy = 0$ generally do not.

exercises.title: Subspace criterion: when is it not a subspace?
exercises.description: Decide whether $U = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid y = x + 1\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and justify your answer.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The question is whether a subset is a subspace. You check three things: zero vector, closure under addition and closure under scalar multiplication. To disprove it, a single counterexample is enough.

Step 2: State the subspace criterion
A subset $U \subseteq V$ is a subspace if (1) $\vec{0} \in U$, (2) $\vec{u}+\vec{v} \in U$ for all $\vec{u},\vec{v} \in U$ and (3) $\lambda\vec{u} \in U$ for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, $\vec{u} \in U$. Failing a single condition is enough to show that $U$ is not a subspace.

Step 3: Test the zero vector
For $\vec{0} = (0,0)$ we would need $0 = 0 + 1$. This is false, so $\vec{0} \notin U$.

Step 4: Second check
Addition also leaves $U$: $(1,2) \in U$ and $(2,3) \in U$, but $(1,2)+(2,3) = (3,5)$ gives $5 \neq 3+1$, so $(3,5) \notin U$.

Step 5: Conclusion
$U$ is not a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Geometrically $U$ is a line that does not pass through the origin. The subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^2$ are only $\{\vec{0}\}$, lines through the origin and $\mathbb{R}^2$ itself.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
The zero-vector test is the fastest way to disprove it. An equation of the form “left side $= c$” with $c \neq 0$ never describes a subspace but a shifted line or plane.

exercises.title: Linear independence using Gaussian elimination
exercises.description: Check whether the vectors $\vec{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{c} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ are linearly independent in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Linear independence means: only the trivial linear combination gives the zero vector. This translates into a homogeneous system of equations that we solve.

Step 2: Set-up
We look for all $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ with $\alpha\vec{a}+\beta\vec{b}+\gamma\vec{c} = \vec{0}$. Only the trivial solution $\alpha=\beta=\gamma=0$ means linear independence.

Step 3: System of equations
Component-wise: $\alpha + \gamma = 0$, $\alpha + \beta = 0$, $\beta + \gamma = 0$.

Step 4: Solve
The first equation gives $\gamma = -\alpha$, the second $\beta = -\alpha$. Substituting into the third gives $-\alpha - \alpha = 0$, so $\alpha = 0$ and hence $\beta = \gamma = 0$.

Step 5: Check with the determinant
The matrix with columns $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ has $\det = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 1\cdot(1-0) - 0 + 1\cdot(1-0) = 2 \neq 0$.

Step 6: Result
The three vectors are linearly independent and therefore even form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are linearly independent exactly when $\det \neq 0$. The system and the determinant give the same statement; the determinant is faster, while the system also reveals a concrete dependence if there is one.

exercises.title: Finding coordinates with respect to a basis
exercises.description: Show that $B = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} \right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and find the coordinates of $\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$ with respect to $B$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The coordinates of a vector are the coefficients of its linear combination of the basis vectors. So first make sure $B$ really is a basis; then solve a linear system.

Step 2: Show it is a basis
Two vectors form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ exactly when they are linearly independent, i.e. when the determinant is non-zero: $\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix} = 1\cdot 5 - 3\cdot 2 = -1 \neq 0$.

Step 3: Coordinate equation
We look for $x,y$ with $x\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + y\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$. This gives $x + 3y = 5$ and $2x + 5y = 9$.

Step 4: Solve
From the first equation: $x = 5 - 3y$. Substituting: $2(5-3y) + 5y = 9 \Rightarrow 10 - y = 9 \Rightarrow y = 1$, so $x = 2$.

Step 5: Check
$2\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + 1\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓

Step 6: Result
$[\vec{v}]_B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The coordinates depend on the chosen basis, the vector $\vec{v}$ itself does not.

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
Always check: compute the linear combination and compare it with $\vec{v}$. Note that the coordinates $(2,1)^T$ are not the vector itself but only its description with respect to $B$.

exercises.title: Basis and dimension of a subspace
exercises.description: Find a basis and the dimension of the subspace $U = \{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x - 2y + z = 0\}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
A subspace described by an equation is parametrised: choose the free variables as parameters and express the others through them. The vectors in front of the parameters form a spanning set.

Step 2: Solve the equation for one variable
From $x - 2y + z = 0$ we get $x = 2y - z$. The variables $y$ and $z$ can be chosen freely.

Step 3: Write a general vector of $U$
$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2y - z \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} = y\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + z\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Spanning set
Hence $U = \operatorname{span}\left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}$.

Step 5: Linear independence
From $y\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + z\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \vec{0}$ the second and third components give $y = 0$ and $z = 0$. So the two vectors are linearly independent.

Step 6: Result
A basis of $U$ is $\left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}$, so $\dim U = 2$. This matches the fact that one equation in $\mathbb{R}^3$ lowers the dimension by 1: $3 - 1 = 2$.

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
Rule of thumb: every independent linear equation lowers the dimension by $1$. One equation in $\mathbb{R}^3$ gives a plane (dimension $2$), two independent equations a line (dimension $1$).

exercises.title: Linear Independence in R³
exercises.description: Examine the linear independence of the vectors $\vec{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{v}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 7 \\ 8 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Calculate the determinant
$\det(\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2, \vec{v}_3) = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 5 & 8 \\ 3 & 6 & 9 \end{vmatrix}$

Step 2: Calculation
$\det = 1 \cdot (5 \cdot 9 - 6 \cdot 8) - 4 \cdot (2 \cdot 9 - 3 \cdot 8) + 7 \cdot (2 \cdot 6 - 3 \cdot 5) = 0$

Step 3: Interpretation
The determinant is 0, so the vectors are linearly dependent

Step 4: Verification
$\vec{v}_3 = 2\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1$

exercises.title: Subspace
exercises.description: Show that $U = \{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x + y + z = 0\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Zero Vector
$\vec{0} \in U$, since $0 + 0 + 0 = 0$

Step 2: Closure under Addition
Let $\vec{u}, \vec{v} \in U$
$(x_1 + x_2) + (y_1 + y_2) + (z_1 + z_2) = (x_1 + y_1 + z_1) + (x_2 + y_2 + z_2) = 0 + 0 = 0$

Step 3: Closure under Scalar Multiplication
Let $\vec{u} \in U, \lambda \in \mathbb{R}$
$\lambda x + \lambda y + \lambda z = \lambda(x + y + z) = \lambda \cdot 0 = 0$

Step 4: Conclusion
$U$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$

exercises.title: Basis of R²
exercises.description: Show that $B = \{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Linear Independence
$\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = -2 \neq 0$

Step 2: Generating System
Let $\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^2$
$\vec{v} = \frac{x+y}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{x-y}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 3: Dimension
$\dim(\mathbb{R}^2) = 2 = |B|$

Step 4: Conclusion
$B$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$

exercises.title: Orthogonal Complement
exercises.description: Determine the orthogonal complement of $U = \text{span}\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Definition
$U^\perp = \{\vec{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \vec{v} \perp \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\}$

Step 2: Dot Product
$\vec{v} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 0 \Rightarrow x + y = 0$

Step 3: Basis
$U^\perp = \text{span}\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\}$

Step 4: Verification
The vectors are orthogonal to $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

exercises.title: A subspace of the polynomial space
exercises.description: Let $P_2$ be the vector space of polynomials of degree $\le 2$. Show that $U = \{p \in P_2 \mid p(1) = 0\}$ is a subspace and find a basis of $U$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Polynomials are vectors: they are added and multiplied by numbers coefficient-wise. So the subspace criterion and the notion of a basis work exactly as in $\mathbb{R}^n$. We check the criteria and then find a basis via the coefficients.

Step 2: Zero vector
The zero polynomial satisfies $0(1) = 0$, so it lies in $U$.

Step 3: Closure
Let $p,q \in U$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $(p+q)(1) = p(1) + q(1) = 0 + 0 = 0$ and $(\lambda p)(1) = \lambda p(1) = 0$. Hence $U$ is a subspace of $P_2$.

Step 4: General element
Let $p(x) = a + bx + cx^2$. The condition $p(1) = a + b + c = 0$ gives $a = -b - c$. So $p(x) = -b - c + bx + cx^2 = b(x - 1) + c(x^2 - 1)$.

Step 5: Basis
Thus $U = \operatorname{span}\{x - 1,\ x^2 - 1\}$. The two polynomials are linearly independent because they have different degrees (from $b(x-1) + c(x^2-1) = 0$ we get first $c = 0$ and then $b = 0$).

Step 6: Result
$\{x-1,\ x^2-1\}$ is a basis of $U$ and $\dim U = 2 = \dim P_2 - 1$. The single condition $p(1) = 0$ removes exactly one degree of freedom.

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
Conditions like $p(1) = 0$ are linear in the coefficients and therefore define a subspace. The condition $p(1) = 1$, in contrast, would not give a subspace because the zero polynomial violates it.

exercises.title: Linear independence with a parameter
exercises.description: For which $t \in \mathbb{R}$ are the vectors $\vec{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ t \end{pmatrix}, \vec{v}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ linearly dependent?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We look for the parameter values at which the three vectors become dependent. This happens exactly where the determinant of the column matrix vanishes. The determinant is a polynomial in $t$; its roots are the critical values.

Step 2: Idea
Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are linearly dependent exactly when the determinant of the matrix of their columns equals $0$.

Step 3: Compute the determinant
$\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & t & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Expanding along the first row: $1\cdot(1\cdot 1 - 1\cdot t) - 1\cdot(0\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 1) + 0 = (1 - t) + 1 = 2 - t$.

Step 4: Root
$2 - t = 0 \iff t = 2$.

Step 5: Check for $t=2$
For $t = 2$ we have $\vec{v}_2 = \vec{v}_1 + \vec{v}_3$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓

Step 6: Result
The vectors are linearly dependent exactly for $t = 2$ and linearly independent for all other $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
For parameter problems always confirm the critical values with a check (here the explicit dependence) and state clearly what holds for all other values.

exercises.title: Extending to a basis
exercises.description: Extend the linearly independent vectors $\vec{u}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\vec{u}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ to a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
A basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ needs three linearly independent vectors. We have two, so exactly one is missing, and it must not lie in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2\}$.

Step 2: Preliminary remark
A basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ consists of $3$ vectors. So we need exactly one more vector $\vec{u}_3$ that does not lie in $\operatorname{span}\{\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2\}$.

Step 3: Choose a candidate
A standard basis vector is often a good candidate. We test $\vec{u}_3 = \vec{e}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Test with the determinant
$\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 1\cdot(1\cdot 1 - 0\cdot 1) = 1 \neq 0$ (lower triangular matrix, product of the diagonal entries).

Step 5: Justification
The determinant is non-zero, so $\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2,\vec{u}_3$ are linearly independent. Three linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ form a basis.

Step 6: Warning
Not every candidate works: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ equals $\vec{u}_1 - \vec{u}_2$, so it lies in $\operatorname{span}\{\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2\}$ and would be unsuitable. This is why one always has to check.

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
The basis extension theorem guarantees that every linearly independent set can be extended to a basis. Which vector works must always be checked, best with the determinant.

exercises.title: Dimension formula for subspaces
exercises.description: Let $U_1 = \operatorname{span}\left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}$ and $U_2 = \operatorname{span}\left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}$ be subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^4$. Determine $U_1 \cap U_2$, $\dim(U_1 \cap U_2)$ and $\dim(U_1 + U_2)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We first determine the intersection $U_1 \cap U_2$ (by equating general elements) and then get $\dim(U_1+U_2)$ from the dimension formula $\dim(U_1+U_2) = \dim U_1 + \dim U_2 - \dim(U_1\cap U_2)$.

Step 2: General elements
$U_1$: $a\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + b\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = (a,\ b,\ a,\ b)^T$. $U_2$: $c\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + d\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = (c,\ c,\ c+d,\ c+d)^T$.

Step 3: Find the intersection
Equate: $a = c$, $b = c$, $a = c + d$, $b = c + d$. From $a = c$ and $a = c + d$ we get $d = 0$. Then $a = b = c$.

Step 4: Intersection space
The elements of the intersection are $(c,c,c,c)^T$, so $U_1 \cap U_2 = \operatorname{span}\left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}$ and $\dim(U_1 \cap U_2) = 1$.

Step 5: Dimensions of the individual spaces
Each has two linearly independent generators, so $\dim U_1 = \dim U_2 = 2$.

Step 6: Dimension formula
$\dim(U_1 + U_2) = \dim U_1 + \dim U_2 - \dim(U_1 \cap U_2) = 2 + 2 - 1 = 3$.

Step 7: Result
$U_1 \cap U_2 = \operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1,1)^T\}$, $\dim(U_1\cap U_2) = 1$, $\dim(U_1+U_2) = 3$. In particular the sum is not direct because the intersection is non-trivial.

Step 8: Takeaway: What to remember
Equating general elements is the standard method for the intersection of spans. The dimension formula saves you from computing the sum explicitly; it follows the principle “subtract what was counted twice”.

exercises.title: Subspaces and Linear Independence
exercises.description: Examine whether the vectors $\vec{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{v}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ are linearly independent and determine the dimension of the subspace they span.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Linear Independence
We examine the equation $\lambda_1\vec{v}_1 + \lambda_2\vec{v}_2 + \lambda_3\vec{v}_3 = \vec{0}$

Step 2: System of Equations
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 \\ \lambda_2 \\ \lambda_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 3: Gaussian Elimination
$\vec{v}_2 = 2\vec{v}_1$, so the vectors are linearly dependent

Step 4: Dimension
$\dim(\text{span}\{\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2, \vec{v}_3\}) = 2$, since $\vec{v}_1$ and $\vec{v}_3$ are linearly independent

exercises.title: Convex Sets
exercises.description: Show that the set $K = \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\}$ is convex and determine its extreme points.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Convexity
Let $\vec{p}, \vec{q} \in K$ and $\lambda \in [0,1]$
$\|\lambda\vec{p} + (1-\lambda)\vec{q}\| \leq \lambda\|\vec{p}\| + (1-\lambda)\|\vec{q}\| \leq 1$

Step 2: Extreme Points
The extreme points are the points on the boundary $\{(x,y) \mid x^2 + y^2 = 1\}$

Step 3: Justification
Every point in the interior can be represented as a convex combination of two other points

Step 4: Parametrization
$\{(\cos(\phi), \sin(\phi)) \mid \phi \in [0,2\pi]\}$

exercises.title: Intersection of Subspaces
exercises.description: Let $U_1 = \{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x + y = 0\}$ and $U_2 = \{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid y + z = 0\}$. Determine $U_1 \cap U_2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Definition
$U_1 \cap U_2 = \{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x + y = 0 \land y + z = 0\}$

Step 2: System of Equations
$\begin{cases} x + y = 0 \\ y + z = 0 \end{cases}$

Step 3: Solution
$y = -x, z = -y = x$
$U_1 \cap U_2 = \text{span}\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\}$

Step 4: Verification
$\dim(U_1 \cap U_2) = 1$

exercises.title: Direct Sum
exercises.description: Show that $\mathbb{R}^3 = U_1 \oplus U_2$ with $U_1 = \text{span}\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\}$ and $U_2 = \text{span}\{\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Sum
$U_1 + U_2 = \mathbb{R}^3$

Step 2: Intersection
$U_1 \cap U_2 = \{\vec{0}\}$

Step 3: Dimension
$\dim(U_1) + \dim(U_2) = 1 + 2 = 3 = \dim(\mathbb{R}^3)$

Step 4: Conclusion
$\mathbb{R}^3 = U_1 \oplus U_2$

exercises.title: Orthogonal Projection
exercises.description: Determine the orthogonal projection of the vector $\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ onto the subspace $U = \text{span}\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Orthonormalization
$\vec{u}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{u}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 2: Projection
$P_U(\vec{v}) = (\vec{v} \cdot \vec{u}_1)\vec{u}_1 + (\vec{v} \cdot \vec{u}_2)\vec{u}_2$

Step 3: Calculation
$P_U(\vec{v}) = \frac{3}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + 3\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 4: Verification
$\vec{v} - P_U(\vec{v})$ is orthogonal to $U$

exercises.title: Gram-Schmidt Process
exercises.description: Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to the vectors $\vec{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{v}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: First Vector
$\vec{u}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 2: Second Vector
$\vec{u}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 3: Third Vector
$\vec{u}_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 4: Verification
The vectors are orthonormal

exercises.title: Dual Basis
exercises.description: Determine the dual basis to the basis $B = \{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Standard Basis
$B^* = \{\varphi_1, \varphi_2\}$

Step 2: Definition
$\varphi_i(\vec{b}_j) = \delta_{ij}$

Step 3: Calculation
$\varphi_1 = \frac{1}{2}(1,1), \varphi_2 = \frac{1}{2}(1,-1)$

Step 4: Verification
$\varphi_i(\vec{b}_j) = \delta_{ij}$

exercises.title: n+1 vectors in ℝⁿ are dependent
exercises.description: Show: any $n+1$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are linearly dependent. Give a dependence relation for $(1,2),(3,4),(5,6) \in \mathbb{R}^2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The equation $c_1\vec v_1 + \dots + c_{n+1}\vec v_{n+1} = \vec0$ is a homogeneous linear system with $n$ equations and $n+1$ unknowns $c_i$. Such a system always has non-trivial solutions.

Step 2: General argument
The rank of the coefficient matrix is at most $n$ (number of rows), the number of unknowns is $n+1$. So there is at least $n + 1 - n = 1$ free variable, i.e. a non-trivial solution. $\blacksquare$

Step 4: Solve
Second minus $2\times$ first: $-2c_2 - 4c_3 = 0 \Rightarrow c_2 = -2c_3$. Then $c_1 = -3c_2 - 5c_3 = 6c_3 - 5c_3 = c_3$. With $c_3 = 1$: $(c_1,c_2,c_3) = (1,-2,1)$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
Consequence: a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ has exactly $n$ elements; more vectors are dependent, fewer do not span the whole space. This is the foundation of the notion of dimension.

exercises.title: Complement: ℝ³ = U ⊕ W
exercises.description: Let $U = \{(x,y,z) \mid x + y + z = 0\}$ and $W = \operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)\}$. Show $\mathbb{R}^3 = U \oplus W$ and decompose $\vec v = (1,2,3)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Direct sum: $\mathbb{R}^3 = U + W$ and $U \cap W = \{\vec0\}$ (equivalently: every vector decomposes uniquely). Additionally one can check dimensions: $\dim U + \dim W = 2 + 1 = 3$.

Step 2: Trivial intersection
An element of $W$ is $s(1,1,1)$. If it lies in $U$ then $3s = 0$, so $s = 0$. Hence $U \cap W = \{\vec0\}$.

Step 3: Decomposing an arbitrary vector
For $\vec v = (a,b,c)$ put $s = \frac{a+b+c}{3}$ and $\vec u = \vec v - s(1,1,1)$. Then $\vec u \in U$ because the coordinate sum of $\vec u$ is $(a+b+c) - 3s = 0$. So $\vec v = \vec u + s(1,1,1)$ with $\vec u \in U$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
$s$ is the mean of the coordinates; the decomposition is unique (direct sum). Here even $W = U^\perp$, so the decomposition is the orthogonal projection onto $U$. A complement is not unique: $\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0)\}$ is also a complement to $U$.

exercises.title: Linear independence of functions
exercises.description: Show that in $C(\mathbb{R})$ (continuous functions) the functions (a) $1, x, x^2$ and (b) $\sin x, \cos x$ are linearly independent.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Functions are linearly independent if $c_1f_1 + \dots + c_nf_n = 0$ (as a function, i.e. for **all** $x$) implies $c_1 = \dots = c_n = 0$. Since the equation holds for all $x$ we may plug in special $x$ values.

Step 2: (a) $1, x, x^2$
From $a + bx + cx^2 = 0$ for all $x$: $x = 0$ gives $a = 0$; $x = 1$ gives $b + c = 0$; $x = -1$ gives $-b + c = 0$. Adding: $c = 0$, then $b = 0$.

Step 3: (b) $\sin x, \cos x$
From $a\sin x + b\cos x = 0$ for all $x$: $x = 0$ gives $b = 0$; $x = \frac\pi2$ gives $a = 0$.

Step 4: Counterexample: dependent functions
$1, \cos2x, \cos^2x$ are linearly dependent: $\cos2x = 2\cos^2x - 1$, so $2\cos^2x - \cos2x - 1\cdot1 = 0$ (non-trivial relation).

Step 5: Takeaway: What to remember
In $C(\mathbb{R})$ the dimension is infinite: $1, x, x^2, x^3, \dots$ are linearly independent. A general criterion is given by the Wronskian determinant. Here too: finitely many suitable $x$ values suffice to prove independence.

exercises.title: Solution space of a homogeneous system
exercises.description: Determine a basis and the dimension of the solution space of $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 0$, $x_1 - x_2 + x_3 - x_4 = 0$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The solution set of a homogeneous system $A\vec x = \vec0$ is a subspace (the kernel of $A$). By the rank–nullity theorem $\dim\ker A = n - \operatorname{rank}A$. We solve the system and read off a basis.

Step 2: Eliminate
Adding: $2x_1 + 2x_3 = 0 \Rightarrow x_3 = -x_1$. Subtracting: $2x_2 + 2x_4 = 0 \Rightarrow x_4 = -x_2$.

Step 3: General solution
Free: $x_1 = a$, $x_2 = b$. Solution: $(a,\ b,\ -a,\ -b) = a(1,0,-1,0) + b(0,1,0,-1)$.

Step 4: Basis and dimension
$\{(1,0,-1,0),\ (0,1,0,-1)\}$ is linearly independent (entries $1$ in different positions) and spanning. $\dim = 2$.

Step 5: Check with the rank–nullity theorem
The coefficient matrix has rank $2$ (the two rows are not proportional). $\dim\ker = 4 - 2 = 2$ ✓. Substituting: $(1,0,-1,0)$: $1 + 0 - 1 + 0 = 0$ ✓ and $1 - 0 - 1 - 0 = 0$ ✓.

Step 6: Takeaway: What to remember
Number of free variables $=$ dimension of the solution space. Each independent equation lowers the dimension by $1$. The solutions are exactly the vectors orthogonal to both rows of $A$.

exercises.title: Trace-free matrices: basis and dimension
exercises.description: Show that $W = \{A \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} \mid \operatorname{tr}(A) = 0\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}$ and find a basis and $\dim W$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Matrices themselves form a vector space (here $\mathbb{R}^{2\times2}$ with $\dim = 4$). The condition $\operatorname{tr}(A) = 0$ is linear, so we expect a subspace of dimension $4 - 1 = 3$. We verify this and give a basis.

Step 2: Show it is a subspace
$\operatorname{tr}(0) = 0$, so $0 \in W$. For $A,B \in W$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ we have $\operatorname{tr}(A+B) = \operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B) = 0$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\lambda A) = \lambda\operatorname{tr}(A) = 0$. So $W$ is a subspace.

Step 3: General matrix in $W$
$A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ with $a + d = 0$, i.e. $d = -a$: $A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & -a \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Decomposition
$A = a\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} + b\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + c\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Put $H = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $E = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $F = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Linear independence
From $aH + bE + cF = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ comparing entries gives $a = 0$ (entry $(1,1)$), $b = 0$ (entry $(1,2)$) and $c = 0$ (entry $(2,1)$).

Step 6: Result
$\{H, E, F\}$ is a basis of $W$ and $\dim W = 3$. This fits $\dim \mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} = 4$ and the single condition $\operatorname{tr}(A) = 0$: $4 - 1 = 3$.

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
A basis is found by writing the general matrix of the subspace as a linear combination of fixed matrices and proving independence by comparing coefficients. The dimension can be estimated beforehand with the rule of thumb.

exercises.title: Proof: linear independence of sum vectors
exercises.description: Let $\vec{u},\vec{v},\vec{w}$ be linearly independent vectors in a real vector space $V$. Prove that $\vec{u}+\vec{v},\ \vec{v}+\vec{w},\ \vec{u}+\vec{w}$ are also linearly independent.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Proofs about linear independence start with a linear combination equal to the zero vector and show that all coefficients must be $0$. The trick: the hypothesis (independence of $\vec{u},\vec{v},\vec{w}$) is applied to the rearranged equation.

Step 2: Proof idea
We take a linear combination of the new vectors that equals $\vec{0}$ and show that all coefficients must be $0$.

Step 3: Set-up
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma \in \mathbb{R}$ with $\alpha(\vec{u}+\vec{v}) + \beta(\vec{v}+\vec{w}) + \gamma(\vec{u}+\vec{w}) = \vec{0}$.

Step 4: Sort by the original vectors
$(\alpha + \gamma)\vec{u} + (\alpha + \beta)\vec{v} + (\beta + \gamma)\vec{w} = \vec{0}$.

Step 5: Use independence of $ec{u},ec{v},ec{w}$
Since $\vec{u},\vec{v},\vec{w}$ are linearly independent, all coefficients must vanish: $\alpha + \gamma = 0$, $\alpha + \beta = 0$, $\beta + \gamma = 0$.

Step 6: Solve the system
Adding all three equations: $2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma) = 0$, so $\alpha+\beta+\gamma = 0$. Subtracting the equation $\beta+\gamma = 0$ gives $\alpha = 0$; similarly $\gamma = 0$ (from $\alpha+\beta=0$) and $\beta = 0$ (from $\alpha+\gamma=0$).

Step 7: Conclusion
Only the trivial linear combination gives $\vec{0}$, so $\vec{u}+\vec{v},\ \vec{v}+\vec{w},\ \vec{u}+\vec{w}$ are linearly independent. $\blacksquare$ (Note: the argument uses that $2$ is invertible in $\mathbb{R}$.)

Step 8: Takeaway: What to remember
Typical structure: set-up, rearrange by the known vectors, use the hypothesis, solve the resulting system. The same structure carries many independence proofs.

exercises.title: Change of basis: coordinates in a new basis
exercises.description: Let $B = \{\vec{b}_1, \vec{b}_2, \vec{b}_3\}$ with $\vec{b}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{b}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{b}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $B$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$. (b) Find the coordinates of $\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ with respect to $B$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
We need the coordinates of $\vec{v}$ in the new basis. With the matrix $M$ whose columns are the basis vectors, the equation is $M\vec{x} = \vec{v}$. First we show that $M$ is invertible (so we have a basis), then we solve.

Step 2: (a) Show it is a basis
With $M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ (columns $\vec{b}_1,\vec{b}_2,\vec{b}_3$) we get $\det M = 1\cdot(1-0) - 0 + 1\cdot(1-0) = 2 \neq 0$. So the three vectors are linearly independent and form a basis.

Step 3: (b) Set-up
We need $x_1,x_2,x_3$ with $x_1\vec{b}_1 + x_2\vec{b}_2 + x_3\vec{b}_3 = \vec{v}$, i.e. $M\vec{x} = \vec{v}$. Component-wise: $x_1 + x_3 = 4$, $x_1 + x_2 = 5$, $x_2 + x_3 = 3$.

Step 4: Solve
Adding all three equations: $2(x_1+x_2+x_3) = 12$, so $x_1+x_2+x_3 = 6$. Hence $x_2 = 6 - 4 = 2$, $x_3 = 6 - 5 = 1$, $x_1 = 6 - 3 = 3$.

Step 5: Check
$3\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + 2\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + 1\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3+0+1 \\ 3+2+0 \\ 0+2+1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓

Step 6: Result
$[\vec{v}]_B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The matrix $M$ converts $B$-coordinates into standard coordinates: $\vec{v} = M[\vec{v}]_B$; conversely $[\vec{v}]_B = M^{-1}\vec{v}$.

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
Remember: standard coordinates $= M\cdot$ ($B$-coordinates). For the opposite direction you need $M^{-1}$. The direction is the most common source of mistakes in basis changes, so always check.

exercises.title: Direct sum: symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
exercises.description: Let $\operatorname{Sym} = \{A \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} \mid A^T = A\}$ and $\operatorname{Skew} = \{A \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} \mid A^T = -A\}$. Show that $\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} = \operatorname{Sym} \oplus \operatorname{Skew}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
“Direct sum” means: every vector can be written in exactly one way as the sum of an element of $\operatorname{Sym}$ and one of $\operatorname{Skew}$. We show existence of the decomposition and that the intersection is trivial.

Step 2: Both sets are subspaces
The zero matrix lies in both sets. From $A^T = \pm A$ and $B^T = \pm B$ we get $(A+B)^T = A^T+B^T = \pm(A+B)$ and $(\lambda A)^T = \pm\lambda A$.

Step 3: Decomposition exists
For arbitrary $A$ let $S = \tfrac12(A + A^T)$ and $K = \tfrac12(A - A^T)$. Then $S^T = \tfrac12(A^T + A) = S$, so $S \in \operatorname{Sym}$, and $K^T = \tfrac12(A^T - A) = -K$, so $K \in \operatorname{Skew}$. Moreover $S + K = A$.

Step 4: The intersection is trivial
Let $A \in \operatorname{Sym}\cap\operatorname{Skew}$. Then $A^T = A$ and $A^T = -A$, so $A = -A$ and hence $A = 0$.

Step 5: Dimension check
$\operatorname{Sym}$ has the basis $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, so $\dim = 3$. $\operatorname{Skew}$ has the basis $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, so $\dim = 1$. Indeed $3 + 1 = 4 = \dim\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}$.

Step 6: Result
Every matrix can be written uniquely as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix: $\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} = \operatorname{Sym} \oplus \operatorname{Skew}$. $\blacksquare$ (The proof works the same way for $n\times n$ matrices.)

Step 7: Takeaway: What to remember
Decomposition criterion: $V = U \oplus W \iff V = U + W$ and $U \cap W = \{\vec{0}\}$. The dimension check $\dim U + \dim W = \dim V$ is a good plausibility test but does not replace the proof.

exercises.title: Dual Spaces
exercises.description: Let $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ and $\varphi: V \to \mathbb{R}$ be a linear mapping with $\varphi(\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}) = 1, \varphi(\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}) = 2, \varphi(\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}) = 3$. Determine the representation matrix of $\varphi$ with respect to the standard basis.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Basis Vectors
$\vec{e}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{e}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 2: Linear Independence
$\vec{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
$\vec{e}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 3: Function Values
$\varphi(\vec{e}_1) = 1$
$\varphi(\vec{e}_2) = 2 - 1 = 1$
$\varphi(\vec{e}_3) = 3 - 2 = 1$

Step 4: Representation Matrix
$[\varphi] = (1, 1, 1)$

exercises.title: Quotient Vector Spaces
exercises.description: Let $V = \mathbb{R}^4$ and $U = \text{span}\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\}$. Determine a basis of the quotient vector space $V/U$ and the dimension of $V/U$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Dimension of U
$\dim(U) = 2$, since the vectors are linearly independent

Step 2: Dimension of V/U
$\dim(V/U) = \dim(V) - \dim(U) = 4 - 2 = 2$

Step 3: Basis of V/U
$\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + U, \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + U\}$

Step 4: Verification
The vectors are linearly independent modulo U and form a basis of V/U
